analysis.investment_thesis: CEAT is a cyclical auto-parts business saddled with rising debt and nine-year net profit CAGR of less than 1%, which disqualifies it as a compounder by my standards. The D/E of 0.68 and promoter holding below 55% are immediate disqualifiers from my framework.
key_strengths: Revenue has grown at a steady 10.3% CAGR over nine years, showing the underlying demand is real
Operating cash flow has been positive all five years, meaning the business does generate cash at the operating level
Strong brand in India's tyre market with OEM and retail channels providing some pricing stability
key_risks: Net profit CAGR of just 0.9% over nine years — revenue is growing but earnings are not; finance costs are compounding at 11.9% and eroding profits
Borrowings nearly doubled from INR 1,792 Cr in FY24 to INR 3,114 Cr in FY25 — aggressive debt-funded capex with uncertain returns
Volatile free cash flow: FCF swings from -337 Cr to +852 Cr year to year, signalling weak earnings quality and heavy working-capital demands typical of commodity-input businesses
red_flags: Debt/Equity of 0.68 — well above my hard ceiling of 0.3; tyre businesses are commodity-input sensitive and should not carry this leverage
Promoter holding at 47.21% — below my minimum threshold of 55%; RPG group has multiple listed entities and capital allocation discipline is uncertain
Finance costs compounding at 11.9% CAGR against revenue growth of 10.3% — debt is growing faster than the business, a structural deterioration
analysis.detailed_analysis: CEAT has a decent franchise in a duopoly-adjacent tyre market, but the economics do not reward patient shareholders. Over nine years, revenues grew 10x faster than net profits, and the reason is clear: finance costs have eaten the incremental operating gains. The sudden jump in borrowings to INR 3,114 Cr in FY25 (from INR 1,792 Cr) suggests a new capex cycle is beginning precisely when FCF dropped to INR 149 Cr — that combination makes me very uncomfortable.
